title: Iran Sets 2‑Day Plan to Reopen Strait, Resume US Nuclear Talks Amid Broader Mideast Updates
body:
Iran’s foreign ministry announced on Monday that Tehran is prepared to roll back its limited closure of the Strait of Hormuz and re‑engage in nuclear negotiations with Washington within a two‑day window, provided the United States meets a series of Iranian demands. The proposal, presented by spokesperson Esmail Baghaei, compresses an earlier seven‑day timeline and signals Tehran’s willingness to use the strategic waterway as a diplomatic lever while seeking relief from economic sanctions that have crippled its oil‑dependent economy.

The plan hinges on a sequence of steps that would see Iran suspend its partial shutdown of the strait – a chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of global oil shipments pass – in exchange for a concrete U.S. response to Tehran’s “core demands.” Those include the unfreezing of Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on its banking sector, and a clear pathway toward the revival of the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA). Baghaei stressed that the two‑day framework is “the basis for negotiation,” indicating Tehran’s readiness to act swiftly if Washington signals a genuine commitment to a diplomatic resolution.

Washington’s reaction is expected to be cautious. While the Biden administration has repeatedly expressed a desire to return to the nuclear deal, it has also warned against any coercive tactics that could destabilize the region. The U.S. State Department has not yet issued an official statement on the latest Iranian overture, but senior officials have underscored the need for “reciprocal confidence‑building measures” before any substantive talks can resume. Analysts note that a rapid reopening of the strait would alleviate immediate shipping concerns, yet it could also embolden Tehran to press for broader concessions, potentially complicating the delicate balance of power in the Gulf.

The backdrop to this development is a series of escalating tensions that began in early April when Iran announced the seizure of several commercial vessels near the strait, accusing them of violating its maritime security. The moves were widely interpreted as retaliation for the United Nations’ decision to renew sanctions on Tehran’s oil exports and a response to the United States’ increased naval presence in the region. The partial closure disrupted oil markets, prompting a modest spike in Brent crude prices and raising alarms among global energy consumers. By offering a rapid de‑escalation, Iran appears to be testing the limits of its leverage while also acknowledging the economic fallout of sustained disruption.

Regional actors are watching the negotiations closely. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, both major oil exporters, have warned that any prolonged interference with Hormuz could trigger a broader crisis affecting global supply chains. Meanwhile, Israel has reiterated its stance that Iran must be held accountable for its nuclear ambitions and its support for militant proxies. The United Nations’ International Maritime Organization has called for calm and urged all parties to respect freedom of navigation, emphasizing that the strait’s stability is vital for international trade.

If the two‑day plan materializes, the immediate effect would be a restoration of normal shipping traffic, easing pressure on oil markets and providing a diplomatic opening for renewed nuclear talks. However, the durability of any agreement will depend on whether Washington can deliver tangible sanctions relief and whether Tehran can demonstrate compliance with nuclear non‑proliferation standards. The coming days will likely see intense back‑channel communications, with both sides weighing the risks of further escalation against the potential gains of a revived JCPOA. As the world watches, the Strait of Hormuz remains a barometer of Middle Eastern geopolitics, and its future trajectory will shape not only regional stability but also the broader landscape of international diplomacy.
